prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "QUANTA SERVICES, INC." (ticker PWR), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PWR", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Quanta Services, Inc.
result.industry: Specialty contracting for electric, gas and energy infrastructure
markets: Electric transmission and distribution construction and maintenance (utilities)
Substations, grid hardening and storm restoration
Power generation construction (renewables, gas, nuclear support)
Electrical and mechanical infrastructure for data centers and large load centers
Underground utility, gas distribution and pipeline services

mission.plain: Quanta says it builds and maintains the infrastructure that delivers power and energy, under the tagline 'Building infrastructure for a brighter future'.

about.plain: Quanta sends skilled crews to build, fix and upgrade the power lines, substations and pipes that carry electricity and gas to homes and businesses. It is the biggest company of its kind in North America, with about 69,500 workers and roughly 80,000 trucks and other fleet units. It also wires up giant data centers and factories and helps build power plants. When storms knock down power lines, Quanta crews are often the ones rushing in to restore power.
about.customers: Mostly electric and gas utilities, plus power producers, data-center and technology companies, manufacturers, pipeline and energy companies.
about.everyday: When the lights come back on after a hurricane, or a new data center that runs your AI chatbot gets power, Quanta crews often did the work.

money.plain: building and maintaining power lines, substations, power plants and data-center electrical systems
gas pipes, pipelines, industrial services and fabrication

money.part: Data center and large-load electrical work
money.plain: wiring and mechanical systems for data centers and factories (Cupertino Electric, Dynamic Systems, Phalcon); share shown is the 2025 Technology, Manufacturing and Communications customer category
making high-voltage circuit breakers with Hyosung HICO (joint venture announced June 2026) to ease equipment shortages

result.summary: Quanta has a real but moderate moat built on scale: it is the largest specialty infrastructure contractor in North America, with about 69,500 employees, its own lineman training college and a record $53.4 billion backlog at June 30, 2026. Utilities return to it for multi-year master service agreements and emergency restoration because few rivals can field skilled crews at that size and safety record. The work is still contracting, so margins are thin (5.7% operating margin in 2025) and rivals such as MasTec, MYR Group and Primoris bid for similar jobs.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue rose 20.3% in 2025 to $28.48 billion and Q2 2026 revenue rose 41.1% to $9.56 billion while gross margin held near 15% (14.8% in 2020, 15.0% in 2025) and Electric segment operating margin reached 11.5% in Q2 2026; scarce skilled labor and a backlog up about 49% year on year support pricing, but much work is bid or done under unit-price and cost-reimbursable contracts, capping margin expansion.

moats.evidence: Quanta is well known to utilities and ranked fifth in its industry on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies scorecard, but it has no consumer brand and customers buy on capability, safety and price.

Utilities embed Quanta in multi-year master service agreements and programmatic grid-upgrade work; its ten largest customers were 30% of 2025 revenue, and replacing a trusted crew base mid-program is costly and risky.
More customers do not make the service more valuable to other customers.

With about 69,500 employees, roughly 80,000 fleet units and $28.5 billion of 2025 revenue (about double MasTec's $14.3 billion), Quanta can staff huge transmission and storm-restoration jobs, self-perform most work and spread equipment, insurance (including captive insurance) and training costs.
Regional utility T&D markets support only a few contractors able to mobilize thousands of qualified linemen, so Quanta, MasTec, MYR, Pike and a few others dominate large programs.

Quanta's 'solutions' model (engineering, supply chain, manufacturing such as the Hyosung breaker JV, and construction under one roof) is harder for single-trade contractors to match, but large EPC firms can copy parts of it.
Decades of energized-line work, safety programs and integration of hundreds of acquired operating companies give it execution know-how on complex high-voltage projects that newer rivals lack.

It owns Northwest Lineman College and the Quanta Advanced Training Center in Texas, giving it a pipeline of scarce skilled craft labor; about 36% of employees are under collective bargaining agreements.

customers.evidence: Large utilities use Quanta repeatedly under multi-year master service agreements; total backlog grew to a record $53.4 billion at June 30, 2026 from $35.8 billion a year earlier, and the largest customer was only 8% of 2025 revenue.

talent.evidence: Quanta trains its own craft workforce through Northwest Lineman College and grew to about 69,500 employees by end-2025, but it does not appear on major best-employer lists and field work is hazardous and cyclical.

product.evidence: It is the largest and most capable grid contractor (Solar Power World named it the top U.S. solar contractor for 2026), but contracting services are hard to benchmark and rivals offer similar services.

threats: A slowdown or pause in AI data-center and utility capital spending, which drove 2025-2026 growth and the stock's premium valuation
Shortage and rising cost of skilled linemen and craft labor
Fixed-price project overruns and execution risk on large transmission, renewable and data-center jobs
Integration risk from a rapid acquisition pace (Cupertino Electric 2024, Dynamic Systems 2025, Phalcon, Enerfab, Percheron and PSD in 2026 for about $1.24 billion upfront)
Utility regulatory or permitting delays to transmission projects and changes to clean-energy policy
Wildfire, storm and workplace safety liabilities on energized-line work
Customer concentration: the ten largest customers were 30% of 2025 revenue
Competition from MasTec, MYR Group, Primoris, Pike and large EPC firms bidding for the same programs

ceo.name: Earl C. "Duke" Austin, Jr.
ceo.background: Fourth-generation utility-industry leader; joined Quanta through its acquisition of North Houston Pole Line; former COO; B.S. in business management and accounting, Sam Houston State University

c1.evidence: Quanta is North America's largest grid and energy infrastructure contractor in a market growing fast on data-center load and grid upgrades, with revenue up 41.1% to $9.56 billion in Q2 2026 and backlog at a record $53.4 billion.

c2.evidence: Utilities choose Quanta for its scale, safety record and in-house craft labor pipeline (Northwest Lineman College, about 69,500 employees), which is hard to copy quickly, but rivals like MasTec, MYR Group and Pike offer similar services.

c3.evidence: Quanta is the default leader among utilities and contractors, but most ordinary people do not recognise the name and it has no consumer product.

c4.evidence: Quanta emphasises 'Building infrastructure for a brighter future' and grid reliability, which matters a great deal over 10 years, but it has no formal published mission statement and its messaging centres on execution and returns.

c6.evidence: “Linemen, power grid, contractor” are the first words for those who know it; impressions are mostly positive (reliable, safety-focused, essential), though most of the public has never heard of it.

c7.evidence: It rides secular trends of rising electricity demand from AI data centers, electrification, grid hardening and aging-infrastructure replacement; Technology, Manufacturing and Communications revenue rose from 6% of revenue in 2023 to 13% in 2025.

c8.evidence: It is expanding from grid construction into data-center electrical and mechanical work (Cupertino Electric, Dynamic Systems, Phalcon), fabrication (Enerfab), engineering (Percheron) and equipment manufacturing (Hyosung HICO breaker JV, up to 800 kV).

m1.evidence: Duke Austin has long argued that utilities face a multi-decade load-growth and grid-replacement cycle and positioned Quanta as a 'solutions' provider, but he is an operator rather than a technology visionary.

m2.evidence: Austin is not the founder (Quanta was formed in 1997) but is a fourth-generation utility-industry leader who has run Quanta since 2016; insider filings show he sold about 156,000 shares in the six months to mid-July 2026 (per Quiver Quantitative).

m4.evidence: Quanta stresses craft-worker safety and training through its own lineman college and training center, and storm-restoration service to utilities, but there is little independent evidence on servant leadership.

m5.evidence: Austin has built a decentralised, craft-focused operating culture across hundreds of acquired companies, but Quanta is a services company rather than an inventor of new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Austin is deeply hands-on with field operations, having come up through North Houston Pole Line and led Quanta's electric and pipeline division, but he has a business and accounting degree rather than an engineering background.

m7.evidence: There is no notable public evidence either way beyond Quanta's safety and community commitments; Austin serves on the Texas State University System Board of Regents.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Duke Austin giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Austin keeps a low public profile focused on operations and is not a widely known personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2016, revenue grew from $7.65 billion (2016) to $28.48 billion (2025) and diluted EPS from $1.26 to $6.80, with 2026 revenue guidance raised to $39.3-39.7 billion.

m10.evidence: Quanta is not publicly known for frugality; SG&A was 7.7% of revenue in 2025 ($2.19 billion).

c10.evidence: Its work keeps electricity and gas flowing to millions of homes and businesses in the U.S., Canada and Australia and restores power after storms, but its reach is regional rather than global.

p2.evidence: Building and maintaining high-voltage transmission lines, substations and energized-line work is dangerous, skill-intensive and essential to the power grid and the AI build-out.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from 2021 to 2025: $12.98B, $17.07B, $20.88B, $23.67B, $28.48B (2020 was $11.20B, after a dip from $12.11B in 2019).

f2.evidence: Margins were broadly flat: gross margin 14.8% in 2020 vs 15.0% in 2025, operating margin 5.5% in 2020 vs 5.7% in 2025.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $6.10 billion vs cash of $0.51 billion, about 3.6x 2025 free cash flow of $1.67 billion, with equity of $9.64 billion and a Moody's upgrade to Baa2.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $611M (2020) to $1,612M (2025) and operating cash flow from $1,116M to $2,230M, though cash flow dipped to $582M in 2021.

v1.evidence: Quanta is the largest and broadest grid contractor, so utilities choose it for scale and reliability on huge programs, but there is no simple product-quality gap an ordinary person would see over MasTec or MYR Group.

v2.evidence: Quanta appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies industry ranking (fifth in its industry) but not on major best-places-to-work lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If Quanta vanished, utilities, data-center builders and the public would notice slower grid upgrades and storm restoration, as it is the largest provider of skilled crews for the North American power grid.
